Most important topics for Java developers: the learning order

1. TypeScript fundamentals
2. Components and data binding
3. Directives and pipes
4. Services and dependency injection

expert.content:
Why Java developers adapt quickly to Angular

• Angular is class-based and strongly typed (TypeScript), with dependency injection, decorators (similar to Java annotations), modules/imports and a layered structure (components, services, models). The mental model of a Spring Boot application maps directly: @Component ≈ a view controller, @Injectable service ≈ @Service, HttpClient ≈ RestTemplate/WebClient, guards ≈ Spring Security filters (for the UI only).
• The differences to learn first: asynchronous code with Observables and signals, immutability of state, and that the browser is untrusted, so authorisation must always be enforced by Spring Boot.

interviewQA: Which Angular topics matter most for a Java developer?

TypeScript, components and data binding, services and dependency injection, routing and guards, reactive forms, RxJS and HttpClient for REST APIs, signals and change detection, then authentication, performance, testing and deployment.
What is the recommended stack for Angular with a Java back end?
Angular with TypeScript and RxJS on the front end, Spring Boot REST APIs on the server, and PostgreSQL or MySQL for data.

topics.name: Introduction to Angular

beginner.content:
What is Angular?

• Angular is a TypeScript-based, opinionated front-end framework maintained by Google, used for building large-scale single-page applications (SPAs).
• Unlike React (a library), Angular is a complete framework: it ships with routing, forms, HTTP client, and dependency injection built in.
• Angular apps are built from components - each with a TypeScript class (logic), an HTML template (view), and CSS (style).

Fresher Notes

  • Angular is a TypeScript-based framework from Google for building single-page applications.
  • An app is built from components, templates, services and modules (or standalone components in recent versions).
  • Create a project with ng new my-app and run it with ng serve.

Worked Example 1

Bootstrap the app.

Worked Example 2

Signals for state.

Practice Exercise 1

A minimal standalone component.

Practice Exercise 2

CLI workflow.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An Angular app starts in main.ts, which bootstraps the root component. The compiler (Ivy) turns each template into instructions that create and update DOM nodes. When something happens (event, timer, HTTP response) Angular runs change detection from the root: bindings are re-evaluated and only changed DOM parts are updated. Zone.js (or signals in zoneless mode) tells Angular when to check.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tooling: ng new, ng generate (component, service, pipe, guard), ng build (production bundle with AOT and tree shaking), ng test, ng lint, ng add for schematics. Configuration lives in angular.json and tsconfig; environments and budgets control builds.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • The Angular CLI generates code (ng generate component), builds, tests and serves the app.
  • Templates use HTML plus Angular syntax: interpolation {{ }}, property binding [prop], event binding (event).
  • Change detection updates the view when data changes; signals make this more precise in modern Angular.

Senior Notes

  • Choose standalone components over NgModules for new code; they reduce boilerplate and improve tree shaking.
  • Angular is opinionated: dependency injection, RxJS, forms and routing come built in, which suits large teams.
  • Plan for performance: OnPush change detection, lazy-loaded routes, trackBy, and bundle budgets.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Beginner mistakes: forgetting to import a standalone component or directive in imports, mutating inputs in children, subscribing without unsubscribing, manipulating the DOM directly instead of using bindings, and putting logic in templates. Let Angular manage the DOM and keep logic in classes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance basics: production builds (AOT, minification), lazy routes, OnPush, @for with track, avoiding expensive template expressions, image optimization (NgOptimizedImage) and deferrable views (@defer) for below-the-fold content.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a feature-based project structure with lazy-loaded features, a core module of singletons (auth, interceptors), shared presentational components, and strict TypeScript settings for safer refactoring.
codeExamples:
src/app/
  core/       auth.service.ts, auth.guard.ts, auth.interceptor.ts
  shared/     ui/button.component.ts, pipes/money.pipe.ts
  features/
    products/ product-list.component.ts, product-detail.component.ts, products.routes.ts
    orders/   ...
  app.routes.ts, app.config.ts

// OUTPUT:
// each feature builds into its own lazy chunk

topics.name: Components & Data Binding

beginner.content:
Data Binding

Angular offers 4 kinds of binding between the component class and its template:
1. Interpolation: {{ value }} - display a value.
2. Property Binding: [property]="value" - set a DOM property.
3. Event Binding: (event)="handler()" - respond to DOM events.
4. Two-Way Binding: [(ngModel)]="value" - keep a form input and a property in sync.

Fresher Notes

  • A component combines a TypeScript class, an HTML template and CSS. The @Component decorator declares its selector, template and styles.
  • Data binding connects class and template: interpolation, property binding [x], event binding (x), two-way binding [(ngModel)].
  • Components pass data with @Input() and notify parents with @Output().

Worked Example 1

OnPush component.

Worked Example 2

Cleanup in ngOnDestroy.

Practice Exercise 1

Input and Output.

Practice Exercise 2

New control flow.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Each component instance has a view. Angular creates it from the template instructions, runs the constructor, sets inputs, calls ngOnChanges and ngOnInit, renders, and during change detection re-checks bindings. When the component is removed, ngOnDestroy runs. Inputs flow down, outputs (events) flow up; this one-directional flow keeps the app predictable.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Modern API: signal inputs (input()), output(), model() for two-way, computed and effect, viewChild, content projection with <ng-content>, host bindings, template reference variables and @ViewChild.

intermediate.content:
Structural Directives - *ngIf and *ngFor

Structural directives change the DOM's structure by adding/removing elements. *ngIf conditionally renders an element; *ngFor repeats an element for each item in a collection.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Control flow in templates: @if, @for, @switch (new syntax) or *ngIf, *ngFor.
  • Lifecycle hooks: ngOnInit, ngOnChanges, ngOnDestroy for setup and cleanup.
  • Use trackBy (or track in @for) so lists update efficiently.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush and immutable inputs for performance.
  • Smart (container) versus presentational components: keep data fetching in containers and display logic in small components.
  • Avoid heavy logic or function calls in templates; use computed values, pipes or signals.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: mutating arrays or objects passed to OnPush children (no re-render), calling functions in templates (runs every check), using index as track key (wrong DOM reuse), subscribing in ngOnInit without cleanup, and large components that do everything. Use immutable updates, computed values, stable ids and small components.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Component performance: OnPush, signals, track keys, @defer, virtual scrolling for very long lists (cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport) and avoiding layout thrash. Profile with Angular DevTools to see which components re-render.
codeExamples:
{{ row.name }}
 // OUTPUT: // 100,000 rows rendered with about 20 DOM nodes

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a list/detail screen with a smart container that loads data and presentational children that only display and emit events, so the children are reusable and easy to test.

topics.name: Services & Dependency Injection

beginner.content:
Services & Dependency Injection (DI)

A Service is a plain TypeScript class that holds logic/data meant to be shared across components (e.g. an API client). Angular's DI system automatically creates and supplies (injects) a service instance to any component that asks for it in its constructor - you never call new yourself.

Fresher Notes

  • A service is a class that holds logic or data shared between components, such as HTTP calls.
  • Mark it with @Injectable({ providedIn: "root" }) and ask for it in a constructor or with inject().
  • Dependency injection (DI) creates and supplies the instance for you.

Worked Example 1

Fake service in a test.

Worked Example 2

Error handling with retry.

Practice Exercise 1

A data service.

Practice Exercise 2

An auth interceptor.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Angular's injector tree resolves dependencies by type token. When a class asks for a service, the injector looks in the element/component injector, then up through parents to the root, creating the instance on first use and caching it per injector. providedIn: 'root' makes a tree-shakable singleton; component-level providers create an instance per component.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Provider options: useClass, useValue, useFactory, useExisting, InjectionToken for configuration, multi providers (interceptors), and inject() in functions. HttpClient returns cold Observables; operators (map, switchMap, retry, shareReplay) shape the stream.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • HttpClient returns Observables; subscribe or use the async pipe in templates.
  • Provide services at root (singleton), at component level (one per component tree) or in route providers.
  • Use interceptors for cross-cutting concerns: auth headers, error handling, logging.

Senior Notes

  • Keep components thin: put data access and business rules in services and test them in isolation.
  • Use injection tokens and interfaces to swap implementations (for example fake API in tests).
  • Avoid manual subscriptions in services; return Observables and let components use the async pipe or takeUntilDestroyed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: unsubscribed Observables, nested subscribes (use switchMap), services holding component state in public mutable fields, circular dependencies, and swallowing HTTP errors. Return Observables, use the async pipe and a central error strategy.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

HTTP performance: cache read-mostly responses, cancel stale requests with switchMap, batch calls, enable compression and HTTP caching headers on the server, and avoid refetching on every navigation.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a token refresh interceptor. On 401 it obtains a new token once (shared among concurrent requests) and retries the failed requests.

topics.name: Routing

beginner.content:
Angular Router

The Angular Router maps URL paths to components, enabling navigation within a single-page app without a full page reload. Routes are declared as an array of path → component mappings.

Fresher Notes

  • The Angular router maps URLs to components. Routes are an array of objects: { path: "products", component: ProductListComponent }.
  • Put <router-outlet> in a template where the routed component should appear, and link with routerLink.
  • Route parameters (:id) are read with ActivatedRoute or the withComponentInputBinding option.

Worked Example 1

Functional guard.

Worked Example 2

Programmatic navigation.

Practice Exercise 1

Route configuration with lazy loading and a guard.

Practice Exercise 2

Reading parameters.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The router parses the URL into a tree, matches it against the route configuration (first match wins), runs guards and resolvers, loads lazy chunks, creates or reuses components, and renders them into the matching router-outlet. Navigation is a pipeline of events (NavigationStart, GuardsCheck, ResolveEnd, NavigationEnd) that you can observe.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: withComponentInputBinding (route data as inputs), withPreloading(PreloadAllModules), withInMemoryScrolling, route data and title, nested children with multiple outlets, canMatch to choose routes by condition, and runGuardsAndResolvers.

intermediate.content:
Route Parameters

Dynamic segments in a route path (e.g. :id) let one route template handle many URLs, with the actual value read via ActivatedRoute.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Features: child routes, redirects, wildcard 404 route, lazy loading with loadComponent/loadChildren, guards and resolvers.
  • Query parameters carry optional state (filters, page) and keep URLs shareable.
  • Use Router.navigate for programmatic navigation.

Senior Notes

  • Lazy load feature routes to keep the initial bundle small, and preload important ones.
  • Guards (canActivate, canMatch) protect routes; remember the server must enforce authorization too.
  • Use resolvers or signals to load data before showing a screen, and handle loading and error states explicitly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: wrong route order (a wildcard before specific routes), forgetting pathMatch: 'full' on empty-path redirects, relying on client guards for security, memory leaks from unsubscribed route observables, and losing state on navigation. Order routes from specific to general and enforce authorization on the server.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Routing performance: lazy load feature areas, preload what users will need next, keep resolvers fast, and cache data in services so back navigation is instant. Check chunk sizes with the build stats.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an admin area guarded by a role check, lazy loaded, with a "leave without saving?" guard on edit screens.

topics.name: Introduction, Architecture and Angular vs React

beginner.content:
What Angular is

• Angular is Google's open-source, TypeScript-based framework for single-page applications. It is a complete platform: components, templates, dependency injection, routing, forms, HTTP client, animations, testing utilities and a CLI, all designed to work together.
• Not to be confused with AngularJS (1.x, JavaScript, end of life). Modern Angular (2+) releases twice a year and has moved to standalone components and signals.
• An Angular app is a tree of components that render templates, get logic and data from services injected by the DI system, and navigate with the router.

intermediate.content:
The building blocks

BlockRoleJava/Spring analogy
ComponentView + logic for one part of the UIController + view template
TemplateHTML with bindings, directives and control flowThymeleaf/JSP page
Directive / PipeChange DOM behaviour / format valuesTag library / formatter
ServiceReusable logic and data access@Service bean
Dependency InjectionProvides services to classesSpring IoC container
RouterMaps URLs to components@RequestMapping
HttpClientCalls REST APIsRestTemplate / WebClient
Guard / InterceptorRoute protection / request pipelineSecurity filter / servlet filter
• Data flows down through inputs and up through outputs; shared state lives in services (or a store).

expert.content:
Angular vs React

AspectAngularReact
KindFull frameworkUI library
LanguageTypeScript (required)JavaScript or TypeScript
TemplatesHTML templates with directivesJSX in JavaScript
ReactivitySignals, RxJS, change detectionState + re-render, hooks
DIBuilt inContext or libraries
Routing/Forms/HTTPOfficial packagesThird-party choices
StructureOpinionated, consistent across teamsFlexible, you decide
FitsLarge enterprise teams, Java/.NET backgroundsFlexible products, huge ecosystem
• Angular's consistency is a strength in big teams; React's flexibility is a strength in small ones. Both are production-proven.

interviewQA: Is Angular a framework or a library?
A framework: it provides components, templates, DI, routing, forms, HTTP and tooling out of the box, in an opinionated structure.
What is the difference between AngularJS and Angular?
AngularJS (1.x) was JavaScript with controllers and scopes and is end of life. Angular (2+) is a TypeScript, component-based rewrite with DI, AOT compilation, standalone components and signals.
How does Angular differ from React?
Angular is an all-in-one, opinionated framework in TypeScript with HTML templates and built-in DI, routing, forms and HTTP; React is a view library using JSX where you choose the surrounding tools.

topics.name: Angular CLI and Project Structure

beginner.content:
The Angular CLI

• Install Node.js (LTS), then npm install -g @angular/cli. The CLI (ng) creates, builds, tests and serves projects and generates code.
• Key commands: ng new app, ng serve (dev server on http://localhost:4200 with live reload), ng generate component|service|pipe|directive|guard (ng g c ...), ng build, ng test, ng update, ng add.
codeExamples:
# create and run
npm install -g @angular/cli
ng new course-portal --style=scss --routing --ssr=false
cd course-portal
ng serve --open                      # http://localhost:4200

# generate code (each creates .ts, .html, .scss, .spec.ts)
ng generate component courses/course-list
ng generate service core/course
ng generate pipe shared/time-ago
ng generate guard core/auth
ng generate interceptor core/auth

ng build --configuration production  # optimised output in dist/
ng test                              # unit tests
ng update @angular/core @angular/cli # upgrade versions

intermediate.content:
Project structure

• src/main.ts bootstraps the app; src/index.html holds <app-root>; src/app/app.config.ts declares application-wide providers (router, HttpClient); app.routes.ts the routes.
• angular.json configures builds; tsconfig.json TypeScript (turn on strict); package.json scripts and dependencies; src/environments or build-time config for environment values; public/ (or assets/) static files.
• Organise by feature, not by file type.

expert.content:
Build, configuration and tooling

• ng serve uses the esbuild/Vite based builder (fast rebuilds); ng build produces hashed, tree-shaken bundles with AOT (ahead-of-time) compilation: templates are compiled at build time, so the browser does less work and template errors appear at build time.
• Strict mode ("strict": true, strictTemplates) catches template type errors early. Keep it on.
• Add ESLint (ng add @angular-eslint/schematics), Prettier, and optionally Angular Material (ng add @angular/material).
• Schematics automate repetitive code and upgrades: ng add installs a library and wires it up.

interviewQA: What does ng serve do?
Builds the app in development mode, starts a dev server (default port 4200) and rebuilds and reloads the browser when source files change.
What is AOT compilation?

Ahead-of-time compilation converts Angular templates and decorators into JavaScript at build time. It makes the app start faster, reports template errors during the build and allows better tree shaking.
How should an Angular project be organised?
By feature (courses, account), with a core folder for singletons (auth, interceptors, guards) and a shared folder for reusable components, directives and pipes.

topics.name: Components, Templates, Data Binding, Directives and Pipes: Overview

beginner.content:
A first component

• A component is a TypeScript class decorated with @Component, which connects it to an HTML template and styles. The selector is the custom HTML tag you use to place it.
• Standalone components (the default in modern Angular) list what they use in imports; no NgModule is needed.
• Create one with ng g c courses/course-card.

intermediate.content:
The four kinds of data binding

DirectionSyntaxExample
Component to view{{ }} interpolation<h1>{{ title }}</h1>
Component to view[property]<img [src]="course.imageUrl">
View to component(event)<button (click)="enroll()">
Both ways[(ngModel)] / [(model)]<input [(ngModel)]="name">
• Directives add behaviour to elements (@if, @for, [ngClass]); pipes format values in templates ({{ price | currency }}).

expert.content:
How a template becomes a page

• Templates are compiled (AOT) into JavaScript instructions that create and update DOM nodes. Angular checks bindings during change detection and updates only what changed.
• Template expressions should be simple, side-effect free and fast: they run often. Avoid calling expensive methods in templates; use signals, computed() or pure pipes instead.
• Reserved characters: use @if/@for blocks (control flow) instead of *ngIf/*ngFor in new code.

interviewQA: What is data binding in Angular?
The synchronisation between component data and the template: interpolation and property binding (component to view), event binding (view to component) and two-way binding with ngModel/model.
What does a standalone component mean?
A component that declares its own template dependencies in its imports array and does not belong to an NgModule. It is the default in modern Angular.
Why avoid calling methods in templates?
Template expressions are re-evaluated on every change detection pass, so expensive methods run repeatedly. Use signals, computed() or pure pipes so values are cached.

topics.name: Variables, Data Types, Interfaces, Type Aliases and Generics

beginner.content:
Typed variables

• TypeScript is JavaScript plus static types, checked at compile time and erased in the output. Angular is written in it, so you cannot avoid it. For a Java developer it feels familiar.
• Declare with const and let; annotate with : type or let inference work. Types: string, number (no int/double split), boolean, bigint, null, undefined, arrays (string[]), tuples, enum, unknown (safe), any (avoid), void, never.

intermediate.content:
Interfaces and type aliases

• An interface describes the shape of an object (like a Java interface/DTO). Mark optional fields with ? and immutable ones with readonly. Interfaces can extends others.
• A type alias names any type: unions, intersections, literals, function types. Use interfaces for object models and type aliases for unions.
• Interfaces and types exist only at compile time: they produce no runtime code.

expert.content:
Generics

• Generics (like Java's <T>) let a function, class or interface work with many types while keeping type safety. Angular uses them everywhere: HttpClient.get<Course[]>(), Observable<T>, signal<T>(), FormControl<string>.
• Constrain with extends; use utility types: Partial<T>, Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Pick, Omit, Record.
• Generics are erased at runtime (like Java's type erasure).

interviewQA: Interface vs type alias in TypeScript?
Both describe shapes. Interfaces can be extended and merged and suit object models; type aliases can also name unions, intersections, tuples and function types. Neither exists at runtime.
any vs unknown?
any switches off type checking. unknown accepts any value but requires narrowing (typeof, instanceof) before use, so it stays type-safe.
How do TypeScript generics compare with Java generics?
They serve the same purpose: reusable, type-safe code. Both are erased at runtime; TypeScript adds structural typing and rich utility types such as Partial and Pick.

topics.name: Classes, Inheritance, Polymorphism and Access Modifiers

beginner.content:
Classes and objects

• TypeScript classes look like Java's: fields, a constructor, methods, getters/setters, static members. Create objects with new.
• Parameter properties shorten constructors: constructor(private name: string) declares and assigns the field. Angular DI uses this heavily.
• Class types are structural: any object with the same shape fits, no explicit implements is required.

intermediate.content:
Inheritance, polymorphism and abstract classes

• extends creates a subclass; super(...) calls the parent constructor; override (with noImplicitOverride) marks overridden methods. Polymorphism: a variable of the base type can hold any subclass and calls the overriding method.
• abstract classes cannot be instantiated and may declare abstract methods; implements makes a class satisfy an interface (a class can implement several).
• Prefer composition and services over deep hierarchies.

expert.content:
Access modifiers

• public (default), protected (class and subclasses), private (class only), readonly (assign once). They are enforced by the compiler only.
• True runtime privacy uses JavaScript's #field syntax. Angular components expose to the template only what the template needs: mark things used only in the class as private, and members used in the template as protected or public.
• Convention: private fields for injected services (private http = inject(HttpClient)).

interviewQA: Is TypeScript private really private?
Only at compile time. The emitted JavaScript still has the property. Use #field for runtime privacy, and never rely on private for security.
What are parameter properties?
A constructor shorthand: constructor(private name: string) declares a field and assigns it in one step. It is how Angular classes commonly receive injected services.
Abstract class vs interface?

An interface only describes a contract and has no runtime code. An abstract class can contain shared implementation and state but cannot be instantiated; a class can extend one class but implement many interfaces.

topics.name: Decorators and Modules (import/export)

beginner.content:
Decorators: Java annotations for TypeScript

• A decorator is a function applied with @name to a class, property, method or parameter, adding metadata or behaviour. Angular's decorators are the equivalent of Java annotations: @Component, @Injectable, @Directive, @Pipe, @NgModule, and older @Input, @Output, @ViewChild, @HostListener.
• Angular reads this metadata at build time (AOT) to wire templates, dependency injection and change detection.

intermediate.content:
Writing a simple decorator

• A decorator is just a function that receives the target (and context) and may replace or wrap it. Understanding this removes the mystery from @Component.
• TypeScript 5 supports standard (ECMAScript) decorators; Angular uses its own compile-time handling, so you rarely write decorators yourself but you will read them constantly.

expert.content:
Modules: import and export

• Every .ts file with an import/export is an ES module with its own scope. Share with export; use with import { X } from './x'. Default export (export default) is possible but Angular code prefers named exports.
• Paths: relative (./, ../) or path aliases (@app/core/auth) configured in tsconfig.json. Barrel files (index.ts) re-export a folder's public API.
• import type { Course } imports only types (erased).
• NgModule (@NgModule) is the older Angular packaging system, different from ES modules; modern Angular uses standalone components and a component's own imports array instead. Do not confuse the two kinds of "import".

interviewQA: What is a decorator in Angular?
A function applied with @ that attaches metadata or behaviour to a class, property, method or parameter. Angular decorators such as @Component and @Injectable play the role of Java annotations.
What is the difference between an ES module import and the imports array of a component?
The ES import loads the TypeScript symbol into the file. The component imports array tells Angular which components, directives and pipes the template may use. A standalone component needs both.
What is a barrel file?
An index.ts that re-exports the public API of a folder so consumers import from one path instead of many deep file paths.

topics.name: Component Creation and Template Binding

beginner.content:
Interpolation and property binding

• Interpolation {{ expression }} renders a value as text (escaped, so safe from XSS). Property binding [prop]="expr" sets a DOM property ([src], [disabled], [value], [hidden]) from an expression.
• Attribute, class and style bindings: [attr.aria-label]="label", [class.active]="isActive", [style.width.px]="width".
• Use property binding, never interpolation, for non-string values such as booleans.

intermediate.content:
Event binding and two-way binding

• Event binding (event)="handler($event)" calls a method when the DOM event fires: (click), (input), (keyup.enter), (submit). $event is the event object (or the emitted value for component outputs).
• Two-way binding "banana in a box" [(ngModel)]="name" combines [ngModel] and (ngModelChange); it requires FormsModule. Components support it with model() signals.
• Read the typed value from the event safely: (input)="onInput($any($event.target).value)" or use a template reference variable (#box).

expert.content:
Template syntax details

• Template statements (event handlers) can have side effects; template expressions (bindings) must not. No new, assignments (except in handlers), ++, chaining with ; in expressions.
• Safe navigation user?.address?.city, non-null user!.name (type-only), nullish ?? work in templates.
• Built-in sanitisation: bound HTML ([innerHTML]), URLs and styles are sanitised against XSS. Bypass only with DomSanitizer for trusted content.
• @let declares a template variable: @let total = price() * qty();.

interviewQA: Interpolation vs property binding?

Interpolation converts the expression to a string and inserts it as text (or an attribute string). Property binding assigns the expression value, with its real type, to a DOM property, e.g. [disabled]="isBusy".
What does [(ngModel)] expand to?
[ngModel]="value" (ngModelChange)="value = $event": a property binding plus an event binding, provided by FormsModule.
Is interpolation safe against XSS?
Yes. Angular escapes interpolated values and sanitises [innerHTML], URLs and styles. Bypassing sanitisation requires DomSanitizer and should be avoided with untrusted input.

topics.name: Component Communication: Input, Output, model() and Template Reference Variables

beginner.content:
Parent to child: input

• Data flows down via inputs. Modern Angular uses signal inputs: name = input<string>(), input.required<T>(), optional transform and alias. Read with name(). The older @Input() decorator still works.
• Inputs are read-only inside the child; never mutate them. Derive values with computed().

intermediate.content:
Child to parent: output and model()

• Data flows up via outputs: the child declares saved = output<Course>() and calls this.saved.emit(value); the parent handles (saved)="onSaved($event)".
• model() creates a two-way signal input: the parent uses [(rating)]="value"; the child reads and writes this.rating.set(5).
• The older API: @Output() saved = new EventEmitter<Course>().

expert.content:
Other ways to communicate and template reference variables

• Template reference variable #name gives access to a DOM element or a child component instance within the template: <input #box> <button (click)="add(box.value)">; #form="ngForm" exports a directive.
• viewChild() / viewChildren() signal queries give the parent's class access to child components and elements (after the view initialises).
• Siblings and distant components communicate through a shared service (with a signal or BehaviorSubject), not through each other.
• Guideline: inputs/outputs for parent-child, services for everything else.

interviewQA: How do a parent and a child component communicate?
The parent passes data down with inputs ([prop] bound to input()) and the child sends events up with outputs (output() and emit), or both with model() for two-way binding.
What is a template reference variable?
A #name declared on an element or component that you can use elsewhere in the same template to read its properties or call its methods.
How do two sibling components share data?
Through a shared injectable service holding the state (a signal or BehaviorSubject), which both inject; neither component references the other.

topics.name: Lifecycle Hooks and Content Projection

beginner.content:
Lifecycle hooks

• Angular creates, updates and destroys components, and calls lifecycle hook methods you implement. In order: constructor (inject dependencies only), ngOnChanges (an input changed), ngOnInit (once, after the first inputs: load data here), ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentInit/Checked, ngAfterViewInit/Checked (view and child components ready: DOM access), ngOnDestroy (clean up).
• Newer APIs: afterNextRender()/afterRender() for DOM work, DestroyRef.onDestroy() for cleanup, effect() for reacting to signals.

intermediate.content:
Choosing the right hook

NeedUse
Inject services, set simple defaultsconstructor / inject()
Load data, start timers, set up after inputs are knownngOnInit
React to a changed input (compare previous/current)ngOnChanges or an effect()/computed() over signal inputs
Access child components or DOM elementsngAfterViewInit, afterNextRender
Release resources (timers, listeners, subscriptions)ngOnDestroy / DestroyRef / takeUntilDestroyed
• Avoid heavy work in ngDoCheck/ngAfterViewChecked: they run on every change detection pass. Do not change bound state in ngAfterViewInit (causes ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked).

expert.content:
Content projection: building flexible components

• Content projection lets a component accept markup from its parent and place it with <ng-content>: the Angular equivalent of slots or React's children.
• Multi-slot projection uses select: <ng-content select="[header]">, select="app-footer", select=".actions". Unmatched content goes to the default <ng-content>. ngProjectAs re-labels content.
• contentChild() / contentChildren() query projected components; ng-template plus ngTemplateOutlet projects templates with context for custom rendering.

interviewQA: Difference between constructor and ngOnInit?
The constructor runs when the class is created and should only set up DI and simple fields. ngOnInit runs once after Angular has set the inputs, which is where initialisation and data loading belong.
What is content projection?
Passing markup from a parent into a child component's template, placed with <ng-content> (optionally multi-slot using select), so components such as cards and dialogs can wrap arbitrary content.
When should you unsubscribe or clean up?
In ngOnDestroy or via DestroyRef/takeUntilDestroyed: clear timers, remove event listeners and unsubscribe from long-lived observables to avoid memory leaks.

topics.name: Structural Directives and Control Flow: @if, @for, @switch

beginner.content:
Built-in control flow blocks

• Since Angular 17 the template uses control flow blocks: @if / @else if / @else, @for (with track, @empty), @switch / @case / @default. They need no imports, are faster than the older directives and have better type narrowing.
• @for requires a track expression (use a unique id): it lets Angular reuse DOM nodes when the list changes.

intermediate.content:
@for context variables and track

• Context variables: $index, $count, $first, $last, $even, $odd. Alias them: let i = $index.
• track c.id identifies items (like React keys). track $index is acceptable only for static lists. Without stable tracking Angular destroys and recreates DOM when the array is replaced, losing focus and input state.
• @let stores an intermediate value; @if (user(); as u) aliases the expression result.

expert.content:
The legacy directives (still in many codebases)

• Before Angular 17: *ngIf, *ngFor and [ngSwitch], imported from CommonModule (or each directive in standalone components). The * is shorthand for wrapping the element in an <ng-template>: that is what makes them structural directives (they add/remove DOM).
• Migrate automatically with ng generate @angular/core:control-flow.
• A custom structural directive injects TemplateRef and ViewContainerRef to create or clear views.

interviewQA: Why does @for require track?
It gives each item an identity so Angular can reuse, move and remove DOM nodes efficiently when the collection changes, preserving state such as focus and typed input.
What is a structural directive?
A directive that adds or removes DOM elements (*ngIf, *ngFor, custom ones using TemplateRef and ViewContainerRef). The control flow blocks @if/@for/@switch replace the built-in ones.
@if vs *ngIf?
@if is built-in control flow: no imports, better performance and type narrowing, supports @else if. *ngIf is the older directive from CommonModule; migration is automatic with a schematic.

topics.name: Attribute Directives: ngClass, ngStyle and Custom Directives

beginner.content:
Class and style bindings

• Attribute directives change the appearance or behaviour of an existing element. The simplest tools are plain bindings: [class.active]="isActive", [class]="classes", [style.color]="color", [style.width.px]="w".
• [ngClass] and [ngStyle] accept strings, arrays or objects for several classes/styles at once. Prefer the direct [class]/[style] bindings in new code, which are faster and more flexible.

intermediate.content:
Custom attribute directives

• Create with ng g directive shared/highlight. Use @HostListener for events on the host element, @HostBinding (or the host metadata) for properties, ElementRef to touch the DOM (sparingly) and input() for options.
• Typical uses: highlight on hover, autofocus, click-outside, tooltips, permission checks, drag and drop, input masks.
• Prefer the host metadata object over the decorators in new code.

expert.content:
Host directives and click-outside

• Directive composition: a component or directive can apply other directives with hostDirectives: [...], reusing behaviour without inheritance.
• A click-outside directive listens on document and emits an output when the click target is outside the host; always remove the listener (DestroyRef).
• Use Renderer2 instead of direct DOM access when you must stay compatible with server-side rendering.

interviewQA: Structural vs attribute directives?
Structural directives add or remove elements from the DOM (@if, @for, *ngIf). Attribute directives change the look or behaviour of an existing element (ngClass, ngStyle, custom highlight).
What are HostListener and HostBinding?
HostListener subscribes to events on the directive's host element; HostBinding binds a host property, class or style to a directive property. The host metadata object is the modern alternative.
ngClass vs [class] binding?
[class.name]="cond" and [class]="obj" are the preferred, lighter bindings; ngClass is the older directive that accepts strings, arrays and objects and needs an import.

topics.name: Pipes: Built-in, Custom, Pure and Impure

beginner.content:
Built-in pipes

• A pipe transforms a value for display: {{ value | pipeName: arg1 : arg2 }}. Pipes can be chained.
• Common built-ins: date, currency, number, percent, uppercase, lowercase, titlecase, slice, json (debugging), keyvalue, async (subscribes to an Observable/Promise and unsubscribes automatically), i18nPlural.
• Import each one used by a standalone component (DatePipe, CurrencyPipe, AsyncPipe, ...).

intermediate.content:
Custom pipes

• Create with ng g pipe shared/time-ago. Implement PipeTransform; transform(value, ...args) returns the formatted value. Mark it standalone: true and import it where used.
• Good pipe candidates: formatting (initials, file size, relative time, truncate), simple filtering of display data. Do business logic and heavy computation elsewhere.

expert.content:
Pure vs impure pipes

• A pure pipe (the default) runs only when its input value or arguments change by reference (primitive value change, or a new object/array). Angular caches the result: very efficient.
• An impure pipe (pure: false) runs on every change detection cycle, even when the input is the same object. Needed when the result depends on mutated data or on external state (like async, json and keyvalue do), but expensive.
• Consequence: a pure pipe on an array does not re-run when you push into the same array. Replace the array (immutable update) or use a signal/computed.

interviewQA: Pure vs impure pipe?

A pure pipe runs only when its inputs change by reference and its result is cached. An impure pipe runs on every change detection cycle, which is needed for mutable or external data but costs performance.
What does the async pipe do?
It subscribes to an Observable or Promise in the template, renders the latest value, triggers change detection on emissions and unsubscribes automatically when the view is destroyed.
Why did my pure pipe not update after I pushed to an array?
Pure pipes re-run only when the input reference changes. push mutates the same array, so the pipe is skipped. Assign a new array or use a computed signal.

topics.name: Services, Dependency Injection and Providers

beginner.content:
Why services?

• Components should be thin: they display data and handle user events. Services hold reusable logic and data access: HTTP calls, authentication, caching, shared state, logging, business rules. A service is a plain TypeScript class marked @Injectable().
• Dependency injection (DI): a component asks for a service and Angular's injector creates and supplies it. This is the same idea as Spring's IoC container with @Autowired constructor injection.
• Generate with ng g service core/course.

intermediate.content:
Providers: telling the injector how to create things

• A provider maps a token (usually the class) to how to build the value. Forms: useClass (another class), useValue (a constant), useFactory (a function, with deps), useExisting (an alias).
• Where to register: @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) (app-wide, tree-shakable: preferred), providers in app.config.ts (bootstrapApplication), in a route's providers, or in a component's providers (new instance per component).
• Non-class values use an InjectionToken (like a qualified bean name): config objects, API URLs, feature flags.

expert.content:
Spring vs Angular DI, side by side

ConceptSpringAngular
Declare a managed class@Service, @Component@Injectable()
RegisterComponent scan / @BeanprovidedIn, providers
Request a dependencyConstructor injectioninject(Type) or constructor parameter
Qualified / named bean@QualifierInjectionToken
Scopesingleton, prototype, requestroot singleton, per-route, per-component
Test double@MockBean{ provide: X, useValue/useClass }
• Programming against the DI system, not new Service(), is what makes code testable and replaceable.

interviewQA: What is dependency injection in Angular?
A design pattern where a class declares what it needs and Angular's injector creates and supplies it, instead of the class creating dependencies itself. It enables loose coupling and easy testing.
What does providedIn: root do?
It registers the service with the root injector as an application-wide singleton, and makes it tree-shakable: it is removed from the bundle if nothing injects it.
When do you use an InjectionToken?
For dependencies that are not classes or that need a named key: configuration objects, API URLs, interfaces (which do not exist at runtime) or multiple implementations.

topics.name: Hierarchical Injectors, Singleton Services and inject()

beginner.content:
The injector tree

• Angular has a hierarchy of injectors: the environment injector tree (root, route-level, set by providers) and the element injector tree (one per component/directive in the DOM). A lookup starts at the requesting component and walks up until a provider is found, else throws NullInjectorError.
• Where you provide a service decides its scope and lifetime: root = one instance for the whole app; route providers = one per lazy route; component providers = a new instance for each component instance (destroyed with it).

intermediate.content:
Singleton services and scoping options

• Singleton: providedIn: 'root' (or listed once in app.config.ts). Use for auth state, API clients, caches, app-wide settings.
• Feature-scoped: provide in a route ({ path: 'admin', providers: [AdminStore], loadChildren: ... }) so the service lives while the feature does.
• Component-scoped: providers or viewProviders on the component for state that must not leak (forms wizard, dialog state, per-row editors).
• Beware of accidentally creating a second instance by providing a root service again in a component's providers.
• Resolution modifiers: inject(Token, { optional: true }), { self: true }, { skipSelf: true }, { host: true }.

expert.content:
The inject() function

• inject(Token) returns a dependency and works in an injection context: field initialisers, constructors, factory functions, functional guards/resolvers/interceptors, and runInInjectionContext(). It cannot be called later inside a method or callback.
• Advantages over constructor injection: less boilerplate, works in functions (guards, interceptors), no constructor-parameter inheritance problems, enables reusable "inject helper" functions.
• Use runInInjectionContext(injector, () => ...) when you must call it outside a context, after capturing inject(Injector).

interviewQA: What are hierarchical injectors?

Injectors arranged in a tree (environment injectors and per-component element injectors). A dependency lookup starts at the requesting node and moves up until a provider is found, so providing a service at different levels controls its scope and number of instances.
How do you create a new service instance per component?
Add the service to the component's providers array (and do not use providedIn root for that class). Each component instance, and its children, then get their own instance.
What is an injection context?

The synchronous execution phases in which inject() is allowed: constructors, field initialisers, provider factories and functional guards/interceptors/resolvers. It is not valid inside later callbacks without runInInjectionContext.

topics.name: Service-to-Service Communication and Shared State

beginner.content:
Services injecting services

• Services can inject other services, forming a layered design: data access (CourseApi uses HttpClient), domain/store (CourseStore uses CourseApi), facade or UI services (NotificationService).
• Keep dependencies one-directional. Circular dependencies (A injects B injects A) throw NG0200; fix by extracting the shared part into a third service or by communicating through events/signals.

intermediate.content:
Sharing state across components

• A root service holding state is the Angular way to share data between unrelated components. Expose read-only signals (or Observables) and mutate only through methods, so changes are traceable.
• Signals (signal, computed) are the simplest option; BehaviorSubject + asObservable() suits stream-heavy code; a store library (NgRx) suits large apps.
• Events between services: a Subject acts as a message bus (events$); use sparingly because implicit flows are hard to follow.

expert.content:
Design guidelines

• Single responsibility: one reason to change per service. Name by role: *Api/*Client (HTTP), *Store/*State (state), *Service (logic).
• No UI in services (no DOM access); use components or Renderer for that. Keep side effects in well-named methods.
• Immutability: never mutate arrays/objects held in signals; produce new ones with update(x => [...x, item]).
• Testing: because everything is injected, replace collaborators with fakes ({ provide: CourseApi, useValue: fakeApi }).
• Prefer facade services to give components one simple API over several back-end services.

interviewQA: How can two unrelated components share data?
Through an injectable singleton service that holds the state (signals or a BehaviorSubject) and exposes it read-only; both components inject the same instance.
What causes a circular dependency error in DI and how do you fix it?
Two services inject each other (NG0200). Extract the shared logic into a third service, or restructure so the dependency flows one way (for example using events or signals).
Why expose asReadonly() or asObservable() from a service?
To prevent consumers from changing the state directly. Only the service's own methods can update it, which keeps state changes centralised and traceable.

topics.name: Angular Router: Configuration, Parameters, Query Parameters and 404

beginner.content:
Routes and navigation

• The Router maps URLs to components so an SPA behaves like a multi-page site without reloads. Define a route table (Routes), register it with provideRouter(routes), render the matched component in <router-outlet> and navigate with routerLink or Router.navigate().
• Route fields: path, component, redirectTo + pathMatch, title, data, children, canActivate, resolve, loadComponent/loadChildren.
• A wildcard route ** placed last handles unknown URLs (404).

intermediate.content:
Route parameters and query parameters

• Path parameters (:id) identify a resource. Read them with ActivatedRoute, or (since v16) bind them straight to component inputs with withComponentInputBinding(): id = input.required<string>().
• Query parameters (?q=angular&page=2) hold optional state like filters, sort and page: queryParams in routerLink/navigate, read via queryParamMap or inputs. Keeping state in the URL makes it shareable and refresh-safe.
• Params are strings: convert numbers. They are observables because the same component instance is reused when only the parameter changes.

expert.content:
Navigation details, titles and server configuration

• router.navigate(['/courses', id]) (array form, safe encoding) or navigateByUrl('/courses/5'). replaceUrl: true avoids adding a history entry (after login).
• Set page title per route (or a TitleStrategy) for accessibility and SEO. Use withInMemoryScrolling to restore scroll and handle fragments; withViewTransitions() for animated transitions.
• PathLocationStrategy (default, clean URLs) needs the server to return index.html for unknown paths, otherwise a refresh on /courses/5 gives a 404: nginx try_files $uri /index.html; Spring Boot: forward non-API, non-file paths to index.html. withHashLocation() avoids the issue (URLs with #).
• For true 404 content, the wildcard component can also set the HTTP status under SSR.

interviewQA: How do you read a route parameter in Angular?
Inject ActivatedRoute and use paramMap (an observable), snapshot.paramMap for a one-off read, or enable withComponentInputBinding and declare an input() with the parameter name.
Why must the wildcard route be last?
The router uses the first matching route. ** matches every URL, so placing it earlier would hide all routes after it.
Why does refreshing a deep link return 404 in production?
With clean URLs the browser asks the server for /courses/5, which is not a file. Configure the server to return index.html for unknown paths so Angular's router can handle them.

topics.name: Child Routes and Lazy Loading

beginner.content:
Child routes and layouts

• A route can have children rendered inside a second <router-outlet> in the parent's template: the pattern for layouts (dashboard shell with a sidebar), tabbed pages and master/detail.
• A route with no component (a "componentless route") only groups children and shares a path prefix, guards, resolvers or providers.
• Relative links inside children (routerLink="settings" or "../") are resolved from the current route.

intermediate.content:
Lazy loading

• By default everything lands in one bundle. Lazy loading splits features into chunks downloaded when the route is first visited, cutting the initial download and startup time.
• Single component: loadComponent: () => import('./reports/reports.component').then(m => m.ReportsComponent).
• A whole feature: loadChildren: () => import('./admin/admin.routes').then(m => m.ADMIN_ROUTES). The feature exports a Routes array; it can also declare its own providers.
• Never import a lazy component class statically elsewhere, or it ends up in the main bundle.

expert.content:
Preloading and measuring

• Preloading strategies download lazy chunks in the background after the first render: PreloadAllModules, NoPreloading (default) or a custom strategy (preload only routes with data: { preload: true }).
• Verify with the browser Network tab (a new chunk-XXXX.js appears on first navigation) and ng build --stats-json plus a bundle analyser (source-map-explorer, esbuild-visualizer).
• Rule of thumb: lazy-load every feature except the landing page and the shell; use @defer for heavy widgets inside a page.

interviewQA: What is lazy loading in Angular?
Loading a route's code only when the user first navigates to it, using loadComponent or loadChildren with a dynamic import(), so the initial bundle stays small and the app starts faster.
What is a componentless route?
A route without a component that only groups child routes, sharing a path prefix, guards, resolvers or providers.
What does PreloadAllModules do?
After the initial render it downloads all lazy-loaded chunks in the background, so later navigation is instant without delaying the first load.

topics.name: Route Guards, Resolvers and Protected Routes

beginner.content:
Functional guards

• A guard decides whether navigation may proceed. Modern guards are functions that use inject() and return boolean, a UrlTree (redirect) or an Observable/Promise of those.
• Types: canActivate (may enter), canActivateChild, canMatch (may this route be matched/loaded: use for role-based lazy routes), canDeactivate (leave with unsaved changes).
• Returning a UrlTree (router.createUrlTree(['/login'])) is the idiomatic redirect.

intermediate.content:
Resolvers: load data before the route activates

• A resolver (ResolveFn<T>) fetches data before the component is created, so the view never renders half-empty. The result is available as route.data (or as an input with component input binding).
• Handle failures inside the resolver (catchError returning a redirect or EMPTY), because a failing resolver cancels navigation.
• Use for essential data of the page; for secondary or slow data prefer loading in the component with a skeleton, or @defer.

expert.content:
Protected routes and the golden rule of security

• A typical protected-route flow: unauthenticated user opens /dashboard → authGuard redirects to /login?returnUrl=/dashboard → after login navigate to returnUrl with replaceUrl.
• On a page refresh the in-memory auth state is empty: initialise it at startup (provideAppInitializer) by calling /api/me so the guard does not wrongly redirect.
• Guards are user-experience, not security. The JavaScript runs in the user's browser and can be bypassed; Spring Boot must authenticate and authorise every request (@PreAuthorize, security filter chain). Treat the Angular guard as a convenience that hides pages the API would reject anyway.

interviewQA: canActivate vs canMatch?

canActivate runs after the route matched and decides whether to enter it. canMatch runs during matching and decides whether the route applies at all, so a lazy chunk is not even downloaded when it returns false.
Are Angular route guards a security feature?
No. They only improve the experience by hiding pages. Because client code can be bypassed, the server (Spring Security) must authenticate and authorise every request.
What is a resolver used for?
To fetch data before a route activates so the component renders with its data ready. It runs before the component is created and the result is available in route data or as an input.

topics.name: Template-Driven Forms

beginner.content:
Forms in the template

• Template-driven forms put the form model in the template using ngModel, with Angular building FormControl/FormGroup behind the scenes. Import FormsModule.
• Good for simple forms (login, search, contact). For complex, dynamic or heavily validated forms prefer reactive forms.
• #f="ngForm" exposes the form; #email="ngModel" exposes a control with valid, invalid, touched, dirty, errors.

intermediate.content:
Validation states and CSS classes

• Angular adds CSS classes to controls: ng-valid / ng-invalid, ng-pristine / ng-dirty, ng-untouched / ng-touched. Style them to show errors only after interaction.
• Built-in validator attributes: required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, pattern, email.
• Every control needs a name attribute inside a form; otherwise ngModel throws.
• Disable native validation with novalidate so Angular's messages are used.

expert.content:
When to use template-driven forms

• Template-driven: little code for simple forms; logic hidden in the template; harder to unit-test; asynchronous, hard to control programmatically.
• Reactive: explicit, immutable-ish model in the class; synchronous access to values; easy dynamic fields, custom/cross-field validators and tests.
• Both use the same underlying classes. Do not mix ngModel and formControlName on the same control.

interviewQA: What module does ngModel require?
FormsModule (imported in the standalone component or NgModule). Reactive forms use ReactiveFormsModule instead.
What are the ng-touched and ng-dirty classes?
ng-touched means the control has lost focus at least once; ng-dirty means its value was changed by the user. They are used to show validation errors only after interaction.
Template-driven vs reactive forms?

Template-driven keeps the form model in the template with ngModel and suits simple forms. Reactive forms define the model in TypeScript, giving explicit control, easy dynamic fields, custom validators and straightforward testing.

topics.name: Reactive Forms: FormControl, FormGroup, FormBuilder

beginner.content:
Defining the form model in code

• Import ReactiveFormsModule. Build the model from FormControl (one value), FormGroup (named controls) and FormArray (list of controls). FormBuilder (fb.group({...}), or fb.nonNullable.group) shortens it.
• Bind in the template: [formGroup]="form", formControlName="email", (ngSubmit)="submit()".
• Forms are typed since Angular 14: form.value is Partial<{...}>; use getRawValue() for the complete value.

intermediate.content:
Working with the form programmatically

• Read/write values: setValue (all fields), patchValue (some), reset(), control.disable()/enable(), get('address.city'), markAsTouched.
• React to changes: valueChanges and statusChanges observables; combine with debounceTime and switchMap for search-as-you-type or dependent dropdowns.
• Nested groups mirror nested objects (address: fb.group({ city, pin })), bound with formGroupName.
• Use updateOn: 'blur' | 'submit' to validate less eagerly.

expert.content:
Typed forms and update strategies

• Use FormBuilder.nonNullable (or new FormControl('', { nonNullable: true })) so reset() returns to the initial value instead of null and the type stays string.
• FormGroup<{ email: FormControl<string> }> types let the compiler check form.controls.email and patchValue.
• unified control state change events (control.events, v18+) expose value, status, touched and reset events in one stream.
• Avoid any-typed forms (UntypedFormGroup) in new code.

interviewQA: FormControl, FormGroup and FormArray?
FormControl tracks one value and its validation state; FormGroup groups named controls into an object; FormArray holds an ordered list of controls (dynamic rows). Together they form a tree.
setValue vs patchValue?
setValue requires every control of the group and throws if one is missing; patchValue updates only the provided fields and ignores the rest.
Why use nonNullable controls?
So the control type is string rather than string | null and reset() restores the initial value instead of setting null, avoiding null checks.

topics.name: Validation, Custom Validators, FormArray, Dynamic Forms and Submission

beginner.content:
Built-in and custom validators

• Built-ins: Validators.required, requiredTrue, min, max, minLength, maxLength, pattern, email, compose.
• A custom validator is a function (control) => ValidationErrors | null: return null when valid, an object { errorKey: details } when invalid. Use a factory function to pass parameters.
• A cross-field validator is applied to the group and reads several controls (password match, date range).
• An async validator returns an Observable/Promise (is this username taken?) and runs only after sync validators pass; debounce it.

intermediate.content:
FormArray and dynamic forms

• FormArray models a variable-length list: invoice lines, phone numbers, quiz options. Add with push, remove with removeAt; iterate in the template with @for and bind with [formGroupName]="i".
• Dynamic forms are generated from metadata (JSON from the server or a config object): loop over field definitions, create controls with validators, and render the right input component by type (@switch).
• Toggle validators when fields become conditional: setValidators, then updateValueAndValidity().

expert.content:
Form submission

• On submit: check form.invalid and call markAllAsTouched() to show every error; disable the button and show a spinner while the request is pending (a submitting signal) to prevent double posts.
• Send form.getRawValue() as JSON with HttpClient.post; on success reset() and navigate; on failure show a message and map server field errors (HTTP 400/422) back with control.setErrors({ server: message }).
• Server-side validation is mandatory; the client only improves the experience.
• Accessibility: label every field, role="alert" on errors, focus the first invalid control.

interviewQA: How do you write a custom validator?

A function that takes an AbstractControl and returns null when valid or an object such as { forbidden: true } when invalid. Use a factory function to pass parameters, and apply it to a FormGroup for cross-field rules.
When do you use FormArray?
For a variable number of similar controls or groups, such as invoice lines or quiz questions, adding and removing them at runtime with push and removeAt.
How do you handle server-side validation errors in a reactive form?
Map the error response to controls with control.setErrors({ server: message }) so they display like client errors, while still validating on the client for faster feedback.

topics.name: HttpClient: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE

beginner.content:
Setting up HttpClient

• HttpClient is Angular's HTTP client (the counterpart of Spring's RestTemplate/WebClient). Register it with provideHttpClient() in app.config.ts (add withInterceptors([...]) and withFetch()).
• Methods return cold Observables: nothing is sent until you subscribe (or use the async pipe / toSignal). Each subscription sends a separate request.
• Type the response with a generic: http.get<Course[]>(url). JSON is parsed automatically (the type is a compile-time promise, not validation).

intermediate.content:
Using the API in components

• Prefer declarative consumption: toSignal(api.list()) or the async pipe, which subscribe and unsubscribe for you. For user actions (create, delete) call subscribe (or firstValueFrom) with next/error handlers.
• HTTP observables complete after one response, so they do not leak; still avoid nested subscribes (use switchMap).
• Show loading and error state; do not leave the UI blank. resource()/httpResource() (Angular 19+) wrap this pattern in signals.

expert.content:
Typed responses, observe options and status codes

• { observe: 'response' } returns the full HttpResponse (status, headers: read Location after a 201 or pagination headers); { observe: 'events' } with reportProgress: true reports upload progress; { responseType: 'blob' } downloads files.
• Map the response to your domain model in the API layer (dates as Date, enums), so components deal with clean types.
• The response generic is a promise to the compiler only. Validate untrusted shapes (Zod) in critical places.
• New in recent versions: httpResource(() => url) is a signal-based GET that reloads when its signals change.

interviewQA: Why must you subscribe to an HttpClient call?
HttpClient returns a cold Observable: the request is only sent when something subscribes (subscribe, the async pipe or toSignal). Without a subscription nothing happens.
How do you send query parameters safely?
Use HttpParams (or the params option with an object) so values are encoded correctly, instead of concatenating strings into the URL.
What does observe: "response" give you?
The full HttpResponse including status and headers, not just the body; useful to read the Location header after a POST or pagination headers.

topics.name: HTTP Headers, Interceptors and Error Handling

beginner.content:
Headers and functional interceptors

• Set headers per request with { headers: new HttpHeaders({...}) } or globally with an interceptor. Typical headers: Authorization: Bearer ..., Content-Type (set automatically for JSON), Accept-Language, X-Request-Id, X-XSRF-TOKEN.
• Interceptors are functions in the request/response pipeline (like servlet filters): HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => next(req). Requests are immutable: use req.clone({...}). Register with withInterceptors([a, b]); order matters (first listed runs first on the way out).

intermediate.content:
Error handling

• Failed requests produce an HttpErrorResponse with status (0 = network/CORS error), statusText, error (parsed body) and message.
• Handle at three levels: the call site (catchError for local recovery or a fallback), a global error interceptor (401, 403, 5xx, network; toasts, redirect to login), and the global ErrorHandler for uncaught exceptions (log to Sentry).
• Retry only idempotent requests and only for transient failures, with backoff: retry({ count: 3, delay: (e, i) => timer(2 ** i * 300) }).
• Do not show raw server messages to users; map status codes to friendly text.

expert.content:
Token refresh and caching in interceptors

• A common pattern: on 401 call /auth/refresh once (share the in-flight request with shareReplay), then retry the original request with the new token. Do not intercept the refresh/login URLs themselves (infinite loop).
• Caching interceptor: keep GET responses in a Map (with TTL) and return of(new HttpResponse(...)) for hits; or use HTTP caching headers.
• Context tokens (HttpContext) let a request opt out: context: new HttpContext().set(SKIP_AUTH, true).

interviewQA: What is an HTTP interceptor?
A function in the HttpClient pipeline that can inspect or modify every outgoing request and incoming response, used for auth headers, logging, error handling, caching and loading indicators.
Why do interceptors use req.clone()?
HttpRequest objects are immutable. To change headers, URL or body you create a modified copy with clone and pass that to next().
What does status 0 mean in an HttpErrorResponse?
The browser could not complete the request: network failure, DNS/connection problem, timeout or a CORS block, so no HTTP status was received.

topics.name: API Integration with Spring Boot, CORS and Authentication

beginner.content:
Angular and Spring Boot together

• Typical architecture: Angular (dev server on port 4200) calls a Spring Boot REST API (port 8080) with JSON. In development use the dev-server proxy so the browser sees one origin; in production serve the built Angular files and the API from the same origin (Nginx in front, or Spring Boot static resources).
• Keep a clear contract: DTOs on the server (records), matching interfaces on the client (or generate them from OpenAPI with openapi-generator/ng-openapi-gen). Use proper status codes: 201 + Location, 204, 400/422 with field errors, 404, 409, 401/403.

intermediate.content:
CORS

• The browser blocks a page from reading responses from a different origin (scheme + host + port) unless the server allows it. It is enforced by the browser and configured on the server. Non-simple requests (JSON body, Authorization header, PUT/DELETE) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request.
• Best: avoid CORS with the dev proxy and a same-origin production deployment. If you need it, configure Spring Security CORS with explicit origins; with cookies use withCredentials: true and allowCredentials(true) with a specific origin (never *).
• A "CORS error" with status 0 in Angular is often really a server error or a missing preflight handler.

expert.content:
Authentication and authorization with Spring Security

• Authentication = who are you; authorization = what may you do. Spring Security authenticates (session cookie or JWT) and enforces roles with @PreAuthorize; Angular only reflects the result in the UI (hide buttons, guard routes).
• Two common designs: HttpOnly session cookie (simplest and safest for same-site apps; add CSRF protection) or JWT (short-lived access token in memory + refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie). Do not keep tokens in localStorage: XSS can read it.
• On startup call /api/me to restore the user; expose user, isLoggedIn, roles from an AuthService with signals; handle 401 centrally in an interceptor.

interviewQA: How do you avoid CORS problems between Angular and Spring Boot?
Use the Angular dev-server proxy in development and serve the front end and API from the same origin in production. Otherwise configure CORS on Spring Boot with explicit origins, methods and headers.
Where should Angular store a JWT?
Keep the short-lived access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. Avoid localStorage because any XSS can read it.
Who enforces authorization, Angular or Spring Boot?
Spring Boot. Angular guards and hidden buttons only improve the experience; every API request must be authenticated and authorised on the server.

topics.name: Observables, Observers, Subscriptions and Promises vs Observables

beginner.content:
The core idea

• RxJS (Reactive Extensions for JavaScript) models asynchronous data as streams. An Observable is a lazy producer of zero or more values over time (HTTP responses, clicks, timers, form changes, WebSocket messages). Nothing happens until someone subscribes.
• An Observer is an object (or callbacks) with next, error and complete. subscribe() returns a Subscription you can unsubscribe().
• Convention: name Observables with a trailing $ (courses$).

intermediate.content:
Cold vs hot, and Promises vs Observables

PromiseObservable
ValuesOne (or an error)Zero, one or many over time
ExecutionEager: starts immediatelyLazy: starts on subscribe
CancellationNot built inunsubscribe() / operators
Operatorsthen/catch/finally100+ (map, filter, switchMap, ...)
Multiple consumersShares one resultEach subscription re-runs (cold) unless shared
Async/awaitYesConvert: firstValueFrom(), lastValueFrom()
• Cold observables (HttpClient) run per subscriber: two subscriptions send two requests. Hot observables (DOM events, Subjects) emit regardless of subscribers. shareReplay(1) turns a cold one into a shared, cached one.

expert.content:
Subscribing safely and subscription cleanup

• Long-lived streams (interval, fromEvent, store selectors, valueChanges, Subjects) never complete: an un-cancelled subscription is a memory leak and keeps handlers running after the component is gone.
• Ways to clean up (best first): the async pipe, toSignal(), takeUntilDestroyed() (v16+), take(1)/first() for one-shot streams, a manual Subscription object unsubscribed in ngOnDestroy, or takeUntil(destroy$) (older pattern).
• HTTP calls complete by themselves and need no cleanup (but may still be cancelled with switchMap).

interviewQA: What is the difference between an Observable and a Promise?
A Promise delivers one value and runs eagerly; an Observable can emit many values over time, is lazy (runs on subscribe), is cancellable and has a rich operator library.
What does cold observable mean?
Each subscription triggers a new execution of the producer, such as a new HTTP request. Use shareReplay or a Subject to share one execution between subscribers.
How do you prevent subscription memory leaks?
Prefer the async pipe or toSignal; otherwise use takeUntilDestroyed, take(1) for one-shot streams or unsubscribe in ngOnDestroy for long-lived streams such as interval, fromEvent and Subjects.

topics.name: Operators: pipe, map, filter, switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, catchError, debounceTime

beginner.content:
pipe() and transformation operators

• pipe(op1, op2, ...) chains operators: pure functions that take an Observable and return a new one. Operators run in order for each value.
• map(fn) transforms each value; filter(pred) lets values through; tap(fn) performs side effects (logging) without changing values; take(n), first(), distinctUntilChanged(), startWith(x), scan((acc, v) => ...) (running state) and reduce.

intermediate.content:
Flattening operators: switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, exhaustMap

• They map each value to an inner Observable (often an HTTP call) and flatten the results. The difference is what happens when a new value arrives while the previous inner request is still running:
OperatorBehaviourUse for
switchMapCancels the previous inner request, keeps the latestSearch-as-you-type, route param loading, "latest wins"
mergeMapRuns all inner requests in parallel, results in completion orderIndependent parallel work (limit with the concurrent argument)
concatMapQueues; runs one at a time in orderOrdered writes, saving sequentially
exhaustMapIgnores new values while one is runningSubmit/login buttons: block double clicks

expert.content:
Error handling and timing: catchError, retry, debounceTime, throttleTime

• catchError((err, caught) => ...) handles an error and returns a replacement Observable (of(fallback), EMPTY, or throwError(() => newError)). Place it inside the inner pipe of switchMap so one failed request does not kill the outer stream (otherwise the search box stops working after the first error).
• retry({ count, delay }) resubscribes on error (use for idempotent calls). timeout(ms) errors when no value arrives.
• debounceTime(ms) emits only after a quiet period (typing); throttleTime(ms) emits at most once per period (scroll, clicks); auditTime, delay, timer, interval.

interviewQA: switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap?

switchMap cancels the previous inner observable (latest wins); mergeMap runs all in parallel; concatMap queues them and runs one at a time in order; exhaustMap ignores new triggers while one is active.
Where should catchError be placed in a switchMap search pipeline?
Inside the inner observable (after the HTTP call) so a failed request returns a fallback while the outer stream stays alive. At the outer level an error would complete the stream.
debounceTime vs throttleTime?
debounceTime waits until the source is quiet for N ms and then emits the last value (search input). throttleTime emits the first value and ignores others for N ms (scroll, rapid clicks).

topics.name: Combining Streams, Subject, BehaviorSubject and the async Pipe

beginner.content:
Combining Observables

• combineLatest([a$, b$]) emits an array of the latest values whenever any source emits (after all have emitted once): filters + data, form fields together.
• forkJoin({ user: user$, courses: courses$ }) waits for all sources to complete, then emits once with the last values: parallel HTTP calls ("load everything for this page"). If one errors the whole thing errors; if one never completes it never emits.
• zip pairs by index; merge interleaves several streams into one; withLatestFrom adds the latest of another stream when the source emits; race takes the first to emit.

intermediate.content:
Subject, BehaviorSubject, ReplaySubject

• A Subject is both an Observable and an Observer: you call next() to push values to all current subscribers (multicast, hot). Use it as an event bus or to bridge callbacks.
• BehaviorSubject<T>(initial) remembers the current value: new subscribers immediately get it; read synchronously with .value. The classic way to hold state in a service (signals now cover most of this).
• ReplaySubject(n) replays the last n values; AsyncSubject emits only the last value on completion.
• Expose asObservable() so outsiders cannot call next().

expert.content:
The async pipe, toSignal and interop

• The async pipe subscribes, marks the view for check on emissions and unsubscribes automatically: the default way to render Observables. Use @if (data$ | async; as data) to avoid several subscriptions to the same source.
• toSignal(obs$, { initialValue }) converts an Observable to a signal (auto-unsubscribe); toObservable(signal) goes the other way. This lets you use RxJS for async flows and signals for state.
• Avoid subscribe() inside subscribe() (callback hell): use flattening operators.
• Avoid BehaviorSubject.value sprinkled around: it hides data flow. Prefer signals for state, RxJS for events and async work.

interviewQA: combineLatest vs forkJoin?

combineLatest emits every time any source emits (after each has emitted once) and keeps going. forkJoin waits for all sources to complete and then emits once with their last values, which suits parallel HTTP calls.
What is a BehaviorSubject and when is it used?
A Subject that holds a current value and gives it immediately to new subscribers. It was the standard way to store observable state in services; signals now cover most such cases.
Why prefer the async pipe over manual subscription?
It subscribes and unsubscribes automatically, triggers change detection, and avoids leaks and boilerplate, so templates stay declarative.

topics.name: Standalone Components and Signals: signal, computed, effect

beginner.content:
Standalone components

• A standalone component (standalone: true, the default since v19) declares its own template dependencies in imports and needs no NgModule. The app starts with bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig).
• Benefits: less boilerplate, clearer dependencies, easier lazy loading (loadComponent), better tree-shaking. Directives and pipes are standalone too.
• Migrate old modules with ng generate @angular/core:standalone.

intermediate.content:
Signals: fine-grained reactive state

• A signal is a wrapper around a value that notifies consumers when it changes. Create with signal(initial), read by calling it (count()), change with set(v) or update(fn). Always replace objects/arrays immutably.
• computed(() => ...) derives a read-only, lazily evaluated, memoised signal: it recomputes only when a signal it read changes. Dependencies are tracked automatically.
• Signals make Angular know exactly which views depend on which state, enabling precise updates and zoneless change detection.

expert.content:
effect(), linkedSignal and the signal-based APIs

• effect(() => ...) runs a side effect whenever the signals it reads change: logging, saving to localStorage, syncing with a non-Angular library, drawing on a canvas. It must be created in an injection context (constructor/field) and is cleaned up automatically.
• Do not use effects to derive state (use computed) or to set other signals in a chain (use linkedSignal, a writable signal that resets from a source). Avoid writing to signals inside effects unless you opt in deliberately.
• Signal-based component APIs: input(), output(), model(), viewChild(), contentChild(); toSignal/toObservable for RxJS; resource()/httpResource() for async data.

interviewQA: What is a signal in Angular?
A reactive value container: you read it by calling it, update it with set/update, and Angular tracks which templates and computed signals use it so only those are updated.
computed vs effect?

computed derives a new read-only value from other signals (lazy and memoised) and has no side effects. effect runs side effects (logging, storage, third-party APIs) when its signals change; it should not be used to derive state.
What changed with standalone components?
Components, directives and pipes declare their own imports and no NgModule is needed. Apps bootstrap with bootstrapApplication and lazy-load with loadComponent.

topics.name: Change Detection and the OnPush Strategy
