beginner.content:
How Angular knows when to update the view

• Change detection (CD) compares template bindings with their previous values and updates the DOM. By default zone.js patches async APIs (events, timers, HTTP) and triggers a CD pass over the whole component tree after each.
• The Default strategy checks every component every time: simple but can be slow in big apps. Template expressions run on each pass, so they must be cheap.
• Use ng.profiler/Angular DevTools to see how often components are checked.

intermediate.content:
OnPush

• changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush tells Angular to check a component only when: (1) an input reference changes, (2) an event originates in the component or its template, (3) a bound signal it reads changes, (4) the async pipe emits, or (5) you call markForCheck().
• It skips whole subtrees that cannot have changed: large performance wins, and it forces good habits: immutable data, signals and the async pipe.
• Common pitfall: mutating an input object/array (items.push(x)) does not trigger OnPush; assign a new reference. Make OnPush your default for every component (set it in the schematic defaults in angular.json).

expert.content:
Zoneless Angular and optimisation tips

• With signals (and the async pipe), Angular does not need zone.js. Zoneless mode (provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection() / provideZonelessChangeDetection()) removes zone.js: smaller bundles, faster, more predictable. It works when views update through signals, the async pipe, markForCheck or event handlers.
• Optimisation checklist: OnPush everywhere; signals for state; @for with track; no heavy methods in templates (use computed/pure pipes); run non-UI timers outside the zone (NgZone.runOutsideAngular); virtual scrolling (cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport) for long lists; @defer for below-the-fold parts.
• Use ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck() sparingly (when updating state from non-Angular code), detectChanges() rarely.

interviewQA: What is the difference between Default and OnPush change detection?

Default checks every component on every pass. OnPush checks a component only when an input reference changes, an event fires inside it, a signal or async pipe it uses emits, or markForCheck is called, skipping unaffected subtrees.
Why does an OnPush component not update when I push into an array input?
OnPush compares input references. push mutates the same array, so the reference is unchanged. Assign a new array (immutable update) or use signals.
What is zoneless Angular?
Running without zone.js: change detection is triggered explicitly by signals, the async pipe, markForCheck and event handlers, giving smaller bundles and more predictable, faster updates.

topics.name: Dynamic Components, View Encapsulation and Deferrable Views (@defer)

beginner.content:
Dynamic components

• A dynamic component is created at runtime rather than written in a template: dialogs, widgets chosen by configuration, dashboards, plugin systems.
• Use ViewContainerRef.createComponent(Type) (returns a ComponentRef: set inputs with setInput(), subscribe to outputs, call destroy()) or the declarative *ngComponentOutlet / NgComponentOutlet.
• Load the component class lazily with import() to keep it out of the main bundle.

intermediate.content:
View encapsulation

• By default component styles are scoped to the component (ViewEncapsulation.Emulated): Angular adds unique attributes (_ngcontent-xyz) to elements and selectors, so styles do not leak out or in.
• Modes: Emulated (default), None (styles become global: use for global theme components only), ShadowDom (native shadow DOM: strict isolation).
• Style projected content or child components deliberately: :host (the component element), :host-context(.dark), CSS custom properties (the clean way to theme), and (avoid) ::ng-deep (deprecated, leaks).

expert.content:
Deferrable views: @defer

• @defer (Angular 17+) lazy-loads parts of a template (a component and its dependencies become a separate chunk) when a trigger fires. It cuts the initial bundle and speeds up first render.
• Triggers: on idle (default), on viewport (visible), on interaction, on hover, on immediate, on timer(2s), or when condition. Add prefetch on ... to download early.
• Companion blocks: @placeholder (before loading starts; keep it the same size to avoid layout shift), @loading (after 100ms; minimum 500ms), @error.
• Only standalone components, directives and pipes referenced inside the block are deferred, and must not be used elsewhere eagerly.

interviewQA: What does ViewEncapsulation.Emulated do?
It scopes component CSS by adding unique attributes to the component's elements and rewriting selectors, so styles do not leak to or from other components. It is the default mode.
What is @defer used for?
To lazy-load part of a template on a trigger (viewport, idle, interaction, timer, condition), with placeholder, loading and error blocks, reducing the initial bundle size and improving first load.
How do you create a component dynamically?

With ViewContainerRef.createComponent(Type), setting inputs via setInput and destroying it when no longer needed, or declaratively with ngComponentOutlet. The class can be loaded lazily with import().

topics.name: Server-Side Rendering (SSR), Hydration and Prerendering

beginner.content:
Why SSR?

• A client-rendered SPA sends an empty shell, then JavaScript builds the page: slower first paint on weak devices and poor for crawlers/link previews. Server-side rendering runs Angular on the server and sends ready HTML, which the browser shows immediately; the app then hydrates it (attaches listeners and state, reusing the DOM).
• Prerendering (SSG) renders routes at build time into static HTML: ideal for public content (marketing pages, course catalogue, docs).
• Add it with ng add @angular/ssr, or ng new app --ssr. It creates a Node/Express server entry (server.ts) and provideClientHydration().
codeExamples:
ng new course-portal --ssr
# or in an existing app
ng add @angular/ssr

# app.config.ts
import { provideClientHydration, withEventReplay } from '@angular/platform-browser';
provideClientHydration(withEventReplay())          // replays user clicks made before hydration finished

# build and run
ng build
node dist/course-portal/server/server.mjs          # serves server-rendered pages on port 4000

# prerender static routes at build time (angular.json: "prerender": true, or a routes file)
ng build --prerender

intermediate.content:
Writing SSR-safe code

• On the server there is no window, document, localStorage, layout or real DOM events. Guard browser-only code: isPlatformBrowser(inject(PLATFORM_ID)), or run it in afterNextRender()/afterRender() (client only).
• Use Angular abstractions (DOCUMENT, Renderer2, Title, Meta) rather than touching globals.
• HTTP on the server: relative URLs need a base URL; TransferState (automatic with provideHttpClient(withFetch()) + hydration) reuses server responses on the client so data is not fetched twice.
• Avoid timers and long-lived subscriptions started during server rendering (they delay the response). Per-request state must not live in module-level variables (shared between users!).

expert.content:
Choosing SSR, SSG or a plain SPA

ModeGood forTrade-offs
Client-side SPALogged-in dashboards, admin toolsSlower first paint, weak SEO
SSRPublic, dynamic, SEO-relevant pages (catalogue with live data)Needs a Node server, more complexity, careful browser-only code
Prerendering / SSGMostly static public pages (landing, docs, blog)Rebuild to update; not for per-user content
Hybrid (route-level render mode)Mix: static landing, SSR catalogue, client-only dashboardConfigure per route with serverRoutes
• For a learning platform: prerender or SSR the public course pages (SEO and link previews) and keep the authenticated learner area client-rendered.
• Incremental hydration (@defer with hydrate on ...) delays hydrating parts of the page until needed.

interviewQA: What is hydration?
After server-rendered HTML is shown, Angular attaches event listeners and state to the existing DOM instead of re-creating it, avoiding flicker and repeated work.
Why does "window is not defined" appear with SSR?
The code runs on the Node server, which has no browser globals. Guard it with isPlatformBrowser, use afterNextRender, or use abstractions such as DOCUMENT and Renderer2.
When would you not use SSR?
For authenticated, highly interactive dashboards where SEO does not matter; a client-side SPA is simpler and avoids running a Node server.

topics.name: Component, Service, Signals and RxJS State

beginner.content:
Where state lives

• Component state: UI-only, short-lived data (is the menu open, current tab, form values). Keep it in the component with a signal.
• Service state: data shared by several components (cart, current user, filters). A root (or feature-scoped) service holds it and exposes read-only signals/observables plus methods to change it.
• Server state: data that belongs to the API (lists, records) with caching/invalidation concerns: a store, httpResource, or a query library.
• URL state: filters, page, selected id belong in the route (shareable, refresh-safe).

intermediate.content:
A signals-based store

• A store service combines state, selectors (computed), and actions (methods). Keep the state in one object signal so updates are atomic and easy to reason about, and make it immutable.
• Loading/error flags travel with the data (status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'), avoiding contradictory booleans.
• Provide it at the feature route when it should be discarded with the feature.

expert.content:
RxJS-based state and choosing an approach

• The classic pattern: BehaviorSubject<State> + asObservable() + selectors with map + distinctUntilChanged + shareReplay. It is more verbose than signals but natural when state changes come from streams (WebSocket messages, debounced search).
• ComponentStore (NgRx) and SignalStore (NgRx Signals) give structured local/feature state with less boilerplate than full NgRx.
ApproachUse when
Component signalsState used by one component
Service + signalsMost shared state; small to medium apps
Service + RxJSStream-heavy state, existing RxJS codebases
NgRx SignalStore / ComponentStoreFeature state needing structure
NgRx StoreLarge apps, many developers, need devtools/time-travel, strict unidirectional flow

interviewQA: Where should shared application state live in Angular?
In an injectable service (or a store) that holds the state in signals or observables, exposes read-only selectors and changes it only through methods. Component-only state stays in the component.
Why keep state immutable?
OnPush change detection, signals and memoised selectors detect changes by reference. Immutable updates make changes detectable, debugging easier and prevent accidental shared mutation.
When is NgRx worth it?

In large applications with many developers and complex state interactions that benefit from a strict, predictable unidirectional flow, devtools and time travel; smaller apps do fine with signal-based services.

topics.name: NgRx: Actions, Reducers, Effects and Selectors

beginner.content:
The NgRx flow

• NgRx is Redux for Angular, built on RxJS. One Store holds the state tree. Components dispatch actions (events describing what happened); reducers (pure functions) compute the new state; selectors read slices; effects handle side effects such as HTTP and dispatch new actions.
• Install: ng add @ngrx/store @ngrx/effects @ngrx/store-devtools. Standalone setup: provideStore(), provideEffects(), provideState() for feature slices.
• Benefits: predictable updates, time-travel debugging (Redux DevTools), testable pure functions. Cost: boilerplate.

intermediate.content:
Effects

• An effect listens to the action stream, performs side effects (HTTP, storage, navigation) and emits new actions. Functional effects (createEffect(() => ..., { functional: true })) use inject().
• Use switchMap for loads (latest wins), concatMap for ordered writes, exhaustMap for logins. Handle errors inside the inner pipe and return a failure action so the effect stream never dies.
• Keep reducers pure: no HTTP, no random, no dates inside reducers.

expert.content:
Selectors and using the store in components

• Selectors are memoised functions that read and derive state (createSelector). They recompute only when their inputs change and make components independent of the state shape.
• Components read with store.select(selector) (Observable) or store.selectSignal(selector) (signal) and dispatch with store.dispatch(action).
• Put derived/combined data in selectors, not in components; test selectors and reducers as plain functions.

interviewQA: What are actions, reducers, effects and selectors in NgRx?

Actions describe events; reducers are pure functions producing new state from state and an action; effects handle side effects such as HTTP and dispatch new actions; selectors are memoised functions that read and derive state.
Why must reducers be pure?
So the same state and action always give the same result with no side effects. That enables time-travel debugging, simple tests and change detection by reference.
Why handle errors inside the inner observable of an effect?
An error that reaches the outer effect stream terminates it, so the effect stops reacting to future actions. catchError inside switchMap/concatMap returns a failure action and keeps the effect alive.

topics.name: NgRx SignalStore and State Normalization

beginner.content:
NgRx SignalStore

• SignalStore (@ngrx/signals) is a lightweight, signal-based store: define withState, withComputed (selectors), withMethods (actions, including async with rxMethod), withHooks. Far less boilerplate than the classic Store, while keeping structure and devtools support.
• Provide it where needed (providedIn: 'root' or in a route/component). Methods change state with patchState.
• Choose it for feature-level state in apps that do not need the full action/reducer ceremony.

intermediate.content:
Normalising state

• Normalisation stores entities in a lookup by id instead of nested copies: { entities: { 1: {...}, 2: {...} }, ids: [1, 2] }. Each fact is stored once, so updating a record changes one place, lookups are O(1), and there are no inconsistent duplicates (the same author embedded in 50 posts).
• Relationships hold ids: course.authorId, course.lessonIds; selectors denormalise (join) for the view.
• NgRx provides Entity (@ngrx/entity: createEntityAdapter) and SignalStore's withEntities for this, with helpers addOne, setAll, updateOne, removeOne, upsertOne.

expert.content:
Server state, caching and avoiding over-engineering

• Much "state" in a CRUD app is a cache of server data. Decide the policy: when is it stale, when to refetch, how to invalidate after a mutation, optimistic updates with rollback.
• Do not push everything into a global store. Colocate state, keep UI state local, derive instead of duplicating, and add a store when the pain is real (many components reading and writing the same data).
• Handle optimistic updates: apply the change to the store first, call the API, roll back on failure and show a message.
• Persist only what is needed (localStorage for preferences) and never secrets.

interviewQA: What is state normalisation?

Storing entities once in lookup tables by id (and referencing them by id elsewhere) instead of nesting duplicate copies. It makes updates consistent and lookups fast; selectors join the data for display.
SignalStore vs classic NgRx Store?

SignalStore is a lighter, signal-based store with state, computed, methods and hooks in one definition and little boilerplate. The classic Store uses actions, reducers, effects and selectors, suited to large apps wanting strict unidirectional flow and devtools.
What is an optimistic update?
Updating the UI/state immediately assuming the request will succeed, then rolling back and informing the user if the request fails, making the app feel instant.

topics.name: Authentication with Spring Security, JWT and Secure Sessions

beginner.content:
Choose a session model

• Server session (cookie): after login Spring Security creates a session and sends JSESSIONID as an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie. Simple, easy to revoke (invalidate the session), JavaScript cannot read the cookie. Requires CSRF protection. Best when Angular and the API share a site.
• JWT: the server issues a signed token; the client sends it in Authorization: Bearer .... Stateless, convenient for multiple services/mobile. Harder to revoke: use short-lived access tokens (5-15 min) plus a refresh token (days) stored in an HttpOnly cookie and rotated on use.
• A JWT is signed, not encrypted: never put secrets in it; always verify signature, issuer, audience and expiry on the server.

intermediate.content:
The Angular side

• Keep the access token in memory (a signal in AuthService), not in localStorage/sessionStorage where XSS can steal it. After a page refresh, call /api/auth/refresh (the refresh cookie is sent automatically) at startup to get a new access token.
• An interceptor attaches the token and, on 401, refreshes once and retries (single in-flight refresh). Log the user out and redirect when refresh fails.
• Logout must call the server to revoke the refresh token/session, then clear client state.
• Use provideAppInitializer to restore the session before the first route guard runs.

expert.content:
Secure session checklist

• Passwords: hash with bcrypt/Argon2 (DelegatingPasswordEncoder), never store plain text; rate-limit and lock out repeated failures; require strong passwords; consider MFA.
• Cookies: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax/Strict; set short idle and absolute timeouts; rotate the session id on login (session fixation protection, default in Spring).
• Tokens: short expiry, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, revoke on logout/password change, use asymmetric keys (RS256/ES256) if several services verify tokens.
• Always HTTPS + HSTS. Never log tokens. Do not put personal data in JWT claims.
• For social login use OAuth2/OIDC (Spring Authorization Server, Keycloak) with the authorisation-code + PKCE flow, not hand-rolled schemes.

interviewQA: Where should the Angular app keep a JWT?
Access token in memory (a signal) and the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. Avoid localStorage because XSS can read it.
Session cookie vs JWT?

Session cookies are simple, revocable and invisible to JavaScript (needs CSRF protection). JWTs are stateless and good across services but are hard to revoke, so use short expiry plus rotating refresh tokens.
Is a JWT encrypted?
No. It is signed (tamper-proof) but its payload is only base64url-encoded and readable by anyone, so never store secrets in it and always validate it on the server.

topics.name: XSS, CSRF and Route Guards vs Backend Authorization

beginner.content:
XSS (cross-site scripting)

• XSS runs an attacker's script in your page (steals tokens and data, acts as the user). Angular is secure by default: interpolation {{ }} escapes values, and bindings to [innerHTML], [src]/[href] and [style] are sanitised (dangerous parts such as <script> and javascript: URLs are removed).
• The danger points: bypassSecurityTrust* (DomSanitizer) on untrusted input, direct DOM access (nativeElement.innerHTML, document.write), eval, building templates from user text, and third-party libraries.
• Add a Content-Security-Policy header as defence in depth.

intermediate.content:
CSRF (cross-site request forgery)

• CSRF makes a victim's browser send an authenticated request to your API from another site; the browser attaches cookies automatically. It matters when authentication uses cookies; token-in-header APIs are not vulnerable the same way.
• Defences: SameSite cookies (Lax/Strict), a CSRF token (Spring Security CookieCsrfTokenRepository sets XSRF-TOKEN; Angular's HttpClient reads it and sends the X-XSRF-TOKEN header on mutating same-origin requests automatically), Origin/Referer checks, and no state change on GET.
• Angular only adds the token for relative/same-origin URLs: use a proxy or same origin rather than absolute cross-origin URLs.

expert.content:
Route guards vs backend authorization

• Guards are not security. Everything in the browser, including guards, role checks and hidden buttons, can be read, modified or bypassed (devtools, replaying requests with curl). They exist for usability: do not show pages the user cannot use.
• Authorization must be enforced on the server for every request: Spring Security rules (hasRole), method security (@PreAuthorize), and ownership checks (a user may edit only their own records; never trust an id sent by the client). Respond 401 (not authenticated) / 403 (not allowed).
• Angular's role is to react to those responses (redirect to login on 401, show "no access" on 403).
• Also remember: do not put secrets (API keys with write access, signing keys) in Angular code or environment.ts: they ship to every visitor.

interviewQA: How does Angular protect against XSS?

It escapes interpolated values and sanitises values bound to innerHTML, URLs and styles. XSS appears when you bypass sanitisation with bypassSecurityTrust*, write to the DOM directly, or use eval-like APIs with untrusted input.
How does CSRF protection work between Angular and Spring Boot?

Spring sends an XSRF-TOKEN cookie; Angular's HttpClient reads it and sends X-XSRF-TOKEN on mutating same-origin requests; the server rejects requests without a matching token. SameSite cookies add another layer.
Why can't route guards secure an application?
Client code is under the user's control and can be bypassed. Only the server can reliably authenticate and authorise requests, so guards are merely a usability feature.

topics.name: Performance: Lazy Loading, Bundle Optimization, Memory Leaks and Production Builds

beginner.content:
Bundle optimisation

• Measure first: ng build --stats-json and a visualiser (esbuild-visualizer, source-map-explorer), Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools. Watch Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS).
• Lazy-load routes (loadComponent/loadChildren), defer heavy widgets with @defer, import only what you use (RxJS operators from 'rxjs', individual lodash functions, date-fns instead of moment), avoid pulling large libraries into the main bundle.
• Budgets in angular.json fail the build when bundles grow. Use NgOptimizedImage (ngSrc, priority) for images, compress with Brotli, cache hashed files long-term.

intermediate.content:
Memory leak prevention

• Leaks come from things that outlive a component: subscriptions to never-completing streams, timers (setInterval), event listeners (window/document), closures in singletons holding component references, third-party widgets not destroyed, detached DOM.
• Fixes: async pipe/toSignal, takeUntilDestroyed(), DestroyRef.onDestroy, ngOnDestroy cleanup, @HostListener/Renderer2.listen (auto-removed) instead of raw addEventListener, destroy() third-party instances.
• Find leaks with Chrome DevTools Memory: take heap snapshots before and after navigating away and back; look for retained component instances and detached DOM nodes.

expert.content:
Change detection tuning and production builds

• OnPush + signals, @for with track, no heavy template methods, cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport for long lists, NgZone.runOutsideAngular for high-frequency non-UI work, zoneless mode, @defer for non-critical UI.
• Production build: ng build (production is the default configuration) enables AOT, tree shaking, minification, dead-code elimination, hashed file names and optimised fonts/CSS. Never deploy ng serve output.
• Environment configuration: file replacement or define; check isDevMode(); remove console noise; upload source maps to your error tracker but do not serve them publicly.
• Add a service worker (ng add @angular/pwa) for caching and offline support; test with Lighthouse.

interviewQA: How do you reduce an Angular bundle size?
Lazy-load routes, defer heavy parts with @defer, import only what you use (tree shaking), replace large libraries, set budgets, analyse bundles with a visualiser, and serve compressed, cached assets.
What are common causes of memory leaks in Angular?
Unsubscribed long-lived observables, uncleared timers, listeners added to window/document and never removed, services retaining component callbacks, and third-party widgets that are not destroyed.
What does a production build do?

ng build runs AOT compilation, tree shaking, minification, dead-code elimination and output hashing, and applies the production configuration (environment values, budgets); it should be what you deploy.

topics.name: Unit, Component, Service and HTTP Testing

beginner.content:
What to test and how

• Angular's TestBed creates a testing module/environment for components and services. Test behaviour: what the user sees and what a service returns, not private implementation.
• Service tests are plain unit tests: create the service (TestBed.inject), call methods and assert. Provide fakes for dependencies: { provide: CourseApi, useValue: fakeApi }.
• Pure code (pipes, validators, reducers, utility functions) needs no TestBed: instantiate and call.

intermediate.content:
Component testing

• Use TestBed.configureTestingModule({ imports: [Component] }) (standalone), createComponent, then interact through the DOM: fixture.nativeElement.querySelector(...), click(), and assert on text and attributes.
• Set signal inputs with fixture.componentRef.setInput('title', 'x'); call fixture.detectChanges() (or await fixture.whenStable()) after changes.
• Replace children and services with fakes for isolation; use provideRouter([]), provideHttpClient() + provideHttpClientTesting() where needed. Prefer user-visible assertions (textContent, roles) over internal fields.

expert.content:
HTTP testing

• Use provideHttpClient() + provideHttpClientTesting() and inject HttpTestingController. It captures requests so you can assert on URL/method/headers/body and flush fake responses (or errors) without a server.
• Always call httpMock.verify() in afterEach to fail on unexpected or unflushed requests.
• Test interceptors through HttpClient; test error handling by flushing a status like 500 or a network error (req.error(new ProgressEvent('error'))).
• For fakeAsync tests use tick() to advance timers (debounce, retry delays).

interviewQA: What does HttpTestingController do?

It intercepts HttpClient requests in tests so you can assert on the request (URL, method, body, headers) and respond with fake data or errors using flush, without a real server. Call verify() to ensure no unexpected requests remain.
How do you test a component with a service dependency?
Provide a fake for the service in the TestBed providers (useValue/useClass), create the component, trigger change detection and assert on the rendered DOM.
Why test pipes and validators without TestBed?
They are plain classes/functions with no framework dependencies, so instantiating and calling them directly is faster and simpler.

topics.name: Test Runners: Jasmine and Karma, Vitest and Modern Testing Practice

beginner.content:
Jasmine and Karma (the classic setup)

• Jasmine is the test framework: describe, it, beforeEach, expect(...).toBe/toEqual/toContain/toThrow, spies (jasmine.createSpyObj, spyOn). Karma is the runner that launches real browsers (Chrome) and reports results. ng test runs them in watch mode.
• Generated *.spec.ts files sit next to the code. Run once for CI: ng test --watch=false --browsers=ChromeHeadless --code-coverage.
• Karma is in maintenance/deprecated status; new Angular projects are moving to Vitest (stable in recent versions) or Jest.

intermediate.content:
Vitest

• Vitest is a fast, Vite-based runner with a Jest-compatible API (describe, it, expect, vi.fn(), vi.spyOn, vi.useFakeTimers()). Runs in Node with jsdom or in a real browser (browser mode, Playwright). Quick startup, instant watch mode, snapshot testing and built-in coverage (v8).
• Recent Angular versions support it through the official @angular/build:unit-test builder (runner: "vitest") and the default for new projects moves in that direction; in older versions use community builders (@analogjs/vitest-angular).
• Test code mostly stays the same: TestBed, HttpTestingController and fixture APIs are unchanged; only matchers/spies change (jasmine.createSpy becomes vi.fn()).

expert.content:
Test strategy, harnesses and end-to-end tests

• Testing pyramid: many fast unit tests (services, pipes, validators, reducers, stores), fewer component tests, a small number of end-to-end tests (Playwright or Cypress) for critical journeys such as login, enrol, pay.
• Use component harnesses (@angular/cdk/testing, Angular Material harnesses) to interact with widgets without depending on markup details.
• Test through the public API and the DOM; avoid brittle fixture.componentInstance.privateField access. Prefer data-testid or roles for selectors.
• Run lint, type-check, unit tests, coverage and build in CI on every pull request. Use coverage to find gaps, not as a target.

interviewQA: Jasmine/Karma vs Vitest?

Jasmine is the framework and Karma the browser runner of the classic Angular setup. Vitest is a faster Vite-based runner with a Jest-like API that newer Angular versions support officially; TestBed code stays almost the same.
What is fakeAsync used for?
It runs test code in a controlled zone where timers and promises are virtual; tick() advances the clock so you can test debounce, delays and retries deterministically without real waiting.
What is a component harness?
An abstraction (from Angular CDK) that exposes a component's behaviour in test code (click, getText, isDisabled) so tests do not depend on internal markup and survive refactoring.

topics.name: Angular CLI Build, Environments, Ubuntu and Nginx Deployment, CI/CD

beginner.content:
Build and environment configuration

• ng build compiles to dist/<project>/browser (static files; with SSR also /server). Build configurations in angular.json (production, staging) control optimisation, budgets, source maps and file replacements for environment files.
• Generate environment files: ng generate environments → src/environments/environment.ts (dev) and environment.prod.ts. Everything in them is public: never store secrets; use them for API URLs and feature flags.
• For "build once, deploy anywhere" load a runtime config.json at start (provideAppInitializer), so the same artifact works in test, staging and production.

intermediate.content:
Ubuntu and Nginx

• Static hosting: copy dist/.../browser to /var/www/javaschoollab; Nginx serves it, falls back to index.html for client-side routes, caches hashed assets and never caches index.html, compresses, and proxies /api to Spring Boot (same origin: no CORS).
• HTTPS with Let's Encrypt (certbot --nginx); firewall (ufw allow 'Nginx Full'); run Spring Boot as a systemd service bound to localhost.
• Release safely: upload to a new release directory, switch a symlink, reload Nginx; keep the previous release for instant rollback.

expert.content:
CI/CD with GitHub Actions or Jenkins

• CI: on every push/pull request run install (npm ci), lint, type-check, unit tests (headless), build. CD: on merge to main build the artifact and deploy to staging, then to production (manual approval).
• GitHub Actions: YAML workflows in .github/workflows, secrets in repository/environment secrets. Jenkins: a Jenkinsfile (declarative pipeline) running on your own agents, popular in Java shops that already run Jenkins for Spring Boot.
• Keep pipelines fast (cache node_modules), fail early, never print secrets, and make deployments repeatable and reversible. Version builds and expose the version for support.

interviewQA: Why must environment.ts not contain secrets?
Its values are compiled into the JavaScript bundle that every visitor downloads. Keep secrets on the server and put only public configuration in the Angular app.
Why does Nginx need try_files $uri /index.html for an Angular app?
Client-side routes such as /courses/5 are not files on the server. The fallback returns index.html so Angular's router can render the route instead of a 404 on refresh or deep links.
What is the difference between CI and CD?
CI automatically builds and tests every change. CD automatically delivers successful builds to staging or production, often with an approval gate for production.

topics.name: Example: Course List with Signals, HttpClient, Search and OnPush

beginner.content:
What you build

• A standalone component that loads courses with HttpClient, keeps UI state in signals (signal, computed), filters by a search input and renders with the new @for/@if control flow.

intermediate.content:
Concepts used

• Signals give fine-grained reactivity: filtered recomputes only when courses or query change. • toSignal bridges an Observable into a signal and unsubscribes automatically. • track c.id makes list updates efficient. • OnPush + signals means the template updates only when signals change.

expert.content:
Server-driven search with RxJS

• For large catalogues search on the server: debounceTime + distinctUntilChanged + switchMap (cancels the previous request).

interviewQA: Why use switchMap for search-as-you-type?
It cancels the previous inner request when a new value arrives, so only the latest search result is used.
What do signals add over plain properties?
Fine-grained dependency tracking: derived values (computed) and templates update only when their signals change, enabling OnPush/zoneless change detection.

topics.name: Example: Reactive Form with Custom and Async Validators

beginner.content:
What you build

• A registration form using typed reactive forms: required/email/min-length validators, a cross-field password confirmation validator, an async "email already used" check and clear error messages.

intermediate.content:
Why this design

• Typed forms (nonNullable.group) give type-safe getRawValue(). • The async validator is debounced with timer + switchMap so it does not call the server on every keystroke, and runs only when sync validators pass. • Group-level validators handle cross-field rules. • Show messages only after touched.

expert.content:
Server errors and reuse

• Map server-side validation errors back to controls (control.setErrors({ server: message })), extract validators into a shared file, and build a small app-field-error component to avoid repeating message markup.

interviewQA: Template-driven vs reactive forms?
Template-driven forms use directives in the template with implicit models; reactive forms define the model in code, are explicitly typed, easier to test and better for complex validation.
Why debounce an async validator?
To avoid a server call per keystroke; typically use timer + switchMap so only the latest value is checked.

topics.name: Real-World Scenario: Admin Area with Lazy Routes, Guards and an HTTP Interceptor

beginner.content:
The scenario

• An admin area that only administrators can open, lazy loaded so normal users never download it, with a token interceptor that adds the auth header and redirects to login on 401.

intermediate.content:
Global error handling and loading UX

• A global error interceptor shows a toast for 5xx errors; a loading interceptor counts in-flight requests to drive a progress bar; a custom ErrorHandler reports unexpected exceptions. Keep security in the server: guards only improve UX.

expert.content: Testing the guard and interceptor

interviewQA: Why are route guards not enough for security?
They only control client navigation; the backend must enforce authorization on every API call.
What does an HTTP interceptor allow?
Cross-cutting handling of all requests/responses such as auth headers, error mapping, loading indicators and logging.

[property] - Property binding, sets a DOM element property
(event) - Event binding, calls a method on a DOM event
[(ngModel)] - Two-way binding between a form input and a property
*ngIf - Structural directive, conditionally renders an element
*ngFor - Structural directive, repeats an element per collection item
@Injectable - Marks a class as available for dependency injection
providedIn: root - Registers a service as a singleton for the whole app

RouterModule - Enables client-side routing between components
routerLink - Directive for SPA navigation without full page reload
router-outlet - Placeholder where the routed component renders
ActivatedRoute - Service to read route parameters and query params
Module (@NgModule) - Groups related components, directives, and services

RxJS Observable - Stream of async values used throughout Angular (HTTP, forms, router)
HttpClient - Angular's built-in service for making HTTP requests
